body_markdown:
A bowl of breakfast cereal can seem like one of the easiest ways to start the day. Many products are promoted as nutritious, high in fiber, low in sugar, or made with natural ingredients. However, a new analysis of 77 breakfast cereals suggests that a nutrition label may not tell the whole story.


The 2026 Clean Label Project cereal study examined a wide range of products, including traditional sugary cereals, organic and natural products, and cereals marketed specifically toward health-conscious consumers. Researchers looked beyond ingredients and nutrition facts to examine potential contaminants, including heavy metals, pesticides, glyphosate, and acrylamide.


The findings highlight an important point for consumers: a cereal can appear healthy based on its ingredients and nutritional profile while still containing detectable environmental or processing-related contaminants.


## Chocolate Cereals Showed Higher Lead Levels


One of the more notable findings involved cereals containing cocoa, chocolate, or cacao. According to the Clean Label Project, these cereals generally contained more than twice the amount of lead found in cereals without those ingredients.


The organization reported that 12 of the 13 chocolate-containing cereals tested had detectable levels of lead.


This does not mean that every chocolate cereal poses an immediate health danger. Detectable contamination and a level that causes acute poisoning are very different concepts. Heavy metals such as lead can nevertheless be a concern because repeated exposure can contribute to cumulative intake over time.


For consumers, the finding provides another reason to avoid relying exclusively on marketing terms such as "natural," "healthy," or "better for you." Looking at the overall ingredients, nutritional value, serving size, and variety of foods in the diet can provide a more complete picture.


## Rice-Based Cereals Raised Arsenic Concerns


The study also identified a significant difference between cereals based on different grains.


Clean Label Project reported that rice-based cereals contained approximately 12 times more arsenic per serving than the rest of the cereal category. Rice can absorb inorganic arsenic from soil and water more readily than many other crops, which is one reason rice products have received attention in food safety research.


Arsenic is naturally occurring in the environment, but inorganic arsenic is considered particularly concerning because long-term exposure can have serious health implications.


The findings do not suggest that consumers need to eliminate rice from their diets. Instead, they underscore the value of dietary variety. Alternating rice-based foods with products made from oats, corn, wheat, or other grains can help prevent a single food source from becoming the dominant contributor to exposure.


## Acrylamide Was Found in Almost Every Cereal Tested


Another major finding involved acrylamide, a chemical that can form naturally when certain carbohydrate-rich foods are cooked or processed at high temperatures.


Clean Label Project reported that all but one of the 77 cereals tested contained acrylamide. The organization also found substantial differences between individual products, with some cereals containing up to 21 times more than others.


The study found that wheat and oat cereals contained approximately 2.5 times more acrylamide per serving than rice or corn cereals.


The presence of acrylamide does not automatically mean a food should be considered unsafe. Exposure depends on factors such as the amount consumed, frequency, and overall diet. However, the large differences between products suggest that manufacturing processes and formulation can influence contaminant levels.


For shoppers, this may be another reason to consider rotating breakfast choices rather than eating the same processed cereal every morning.


## Four Cereals Received Recognition


The Clean Label Project did not evaluate cereals solely on contaminant levels. Its 2026 Back-to-School Honor Roll considered several factors, including contaminant testing, added sugar, artificial ingredients, protein, fiber, and healthy fats.


Four products were recognized by the organization: Arrowhead Mills Puffed Kamut, Lovebird Cinnamon O's, Love Grown Power O's Original, and Three Wishes Cinnamon.


It is important to understand what this recognition means. Being included on the Honor Roll does not mean a product is completely free of contaminants or that it is universally the healthiest breakfast choice. Rather, the organization said the products performed relatively well across a combination of nutritional and contaminant-related criteria.


Consumers should therefore treat such lists as one source of information rather than a substitute for reading food labels or considering individual dietary needs.


## What Should Shoppers Look for When Buying Cereal?


The study offers several practical considerations for people shopping for breakfast foods.


First, consumers may want to limit frequent reliance on chocolate or cocoa-based cereals if they are concerned about lead exposure. This does not necessarily require eliminating chocolate completely. Variety can be a useful approach.


Second, consider varying the grains used in breakfast foods. Instead of consuming rice-based cereal every day, families can rotate between different grain options.


Third, pay attention to the nutritional profile. A product with low contaminant levels is not automatically nutritious. Some cereals can be relatively low in certain contaminants while also being high in added sugar and low in protein or fiber.


Finally, consumers interested in contaminant testing can look for products carrying reputable third-party certifications. Such certifications may indicate that products have undergone additional testing, although shoppers should still review what a particular certification actually covers.


## A Broader Lesson About "Healthy" Food


Perhaps the most important takeaway from the study is that the word "healthy" can describe only part of a food's overall profile.


Nutrition, ingredients, processing methods, contaminants, portion size, and dietary patterns all matter. A cereal containing whole grains and added vitamins may provide useful nutrients, but that does not necessarily tell consumers everything about potential environmental contaminants.


At the same time, the presence of a contaminant in a tested product should not automatically lead to fear or panic. Laboratory detection is not the same thing as demonstrating that a food causes illness at normal consumption levels.


The study itself shows why comparisons between individual products can be useful. Contaminant levels varied considerably, demonstrating that consumers may have choices within the same food category.


For families preparing for the new school year, the practical message is relatively straightforward. Breakfast cereal can remain a convenient option, but it does not have to be the only option. Rotating foods, choosing products with stronger nutritional profiles, limiting excessive added sugar, and maintaining dietary variety can all contribute to a more balanced approach to breakfast.


The research also highlights the continuing importance of independent food testing. As consumers increasingly look for foods marketed as clean, natural, organic, or healthy, testing beyond the ingredient list can provide additional information about what is actually present in the finished product.

### Disclaimer


This article is for general informational purposes only and is not medical or dietary advice. The findings described above come primarily from the Clean Label Project's testing and should not be interpreted as proof that a particular cereal is unsafe to eat. Individual dietary needs vary. Anyone with specific concerns about heavy-metal exposure, food safety, or a child's diet should consult a qualified healthcare professional or registered dietitian.
